newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya sets lower inflation as main target.
newsitem.headline: Kenya sets lower inflation as main target.

text.p: The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) has put lowering inflation on top of its agenda in the 12 months ending June 1998, the bank said in a statement on Monday.
In its first monetary policy statement, the bank said: "This is the best contribution the central bank can make to both economic growth and improved distribution of income."
The bank said strict application of tight fiscal policy, especially aiming at a surplus in the budget, would be a determining factor in obtaining desired results.

"Thus, effective management of underlying inflation, particularly confining it to single-digit target at the end of June 1998, will be facilitated by the implementation of the amended Central Bank of Kenya Act (1996)," the bank added.
Kenya's overall average annual inflation stood at 12.3 percent in May from 10.7 percent in March and 4.4 percent in May 1997. Kenyan authorities have blamed drought for the rise.
The amended Act gives the central bank greater autonomy, limits government borrowing from the central bank and gives the CBK governor two four-year secure terms in office.

"Critical to achieving the low single-digit inflation objective will be the observation of the limit on government borrowing from the CBK to no more than 5.0 percent of the most recent audited government gross recurrent revenue," it said.
The bank said that in the fiscal year to June 1998, that translated to 6.0 billion shillings ($109.09 million).

The statement said that the bank would ensure that the expansion of money supply (M3) -- currency outside banking institutions plus the deposits of both the private and other public sectors with the institutions -- eased to no more than 11 percent in the year to June 1998 from 13.5 percent in April.

The statement said government borrowing from domestic sources was expected to decline, reducing the current 128 billion shillings in debt stock by at least 10 billion shillings by the end of June 1998.
It said the central bank would seek to maintain foreign exchange reserves sufficient to cover four months of imports and manage stability in the forex market through June 1998.
Central Bank of Kenya Governor Micah Cheserem told Reuters at a briefing that major movements in the shiling rates versus the dollar were not likely unless huge turmoil hit the country.
He added that he did not see elections later this year as posing any significant threat to the stability of the shilling.
He said interest rates on benchmark 91-day treasury bills were expected to continue a gradual decline in coming months.
Rates were quoted at 19.2 percent last week from a high of around 24 percent in the same period last year.
